title: When You Don’t Believe People Have the Potential to Succeed
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article grapples with the dilemma leaders face when a team member's aspirations exceed their apparent talent: whether to deliver a blunt verdict about their potential or focus feedback narrowly on current skills. The piece argues leaders are frequently wrong about what people can achieve over time, and that pronouncing a negative verdict on someone's potential risks destroying their confidence without actually being accurate. Its recommended approach separates the aspiration from the skill gap — describing specifically what's needed to close the gap now, without commenting on supposedly fixed traits like aptitude or creativity — leaving room for the person's own growth and initiative to prove the leader wrong.
points: Leaders are frequently wrong about a team member's long-term potential — many people prove doubters wrong over time.
Delivering a verdict that someone lacks the potential to succeed risks destroying confidence without being reliably accurate.
The better approach separates the aspiration from the current skill gap, focusing feedback on specific, addressable skills rather than fixed traits.
Good leaders stay focused on what a team member can work on now rather than predicting their long-term ceiling.
